newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerians vote on draft constitution.
newsitem.headline: Algerians vote on draft constitution.

text.p: Algerians began voting on Thursday in a controversial referendum on a draft constitution banning Moslem fundamentalists from gaining power despite calls for a boycott by the opposition.
The official media said turnout was high and that voting was taking place peacefully.

The Armed Islamic Group or GIA -- most feared of the country's Moslem guerrilla movements -- has warned people not to vote, threatening to slit the throats of anyone who leaves home on referendum day.

Three hours after polls opened nearly 23 percent of more than 16 million eligible voters had cast their ballots, Algerian radio quoted the interior ministry as saying. Most of the electorates vote usually after midday.

President Liamine Zeroual, who cast his ballot early in the day at Ghazali school polling station near the presidential palace in Algiers, vowed to respect voters' decision on his proposed constitutional reforms.
"The Algerian people is sovereign. Its will would be respected," a smiling Zeroual told reporters after he voted amid tight security.

Many voters were seen queuing outside polling stations in central Algiers, witnesses said by telephone. Algerian state television showed polling stations opening in the southwestern town of Bechar more than an hour before voting.
Police and paramilitary forces were seen patrolling Algiers streets under drizzling rain, witnesses said.
Stringent security measures have been put in place before the vote to guard more than 35,000 polling stations in a land five times the size of France.
The government has shut schools and turned them into heavy fortified polling stations ringed by soliders in gear combat.
Big city markets have been shut for the week and patrolled by thousands of paratroopers, police and paramilitary forces.
The draft charter would bar Moslem fundamentalists -- whose impending victory at the polls led the authorities to scrap a general election in 1992 -- from seeking power through the political system.

More than 60,000 people have died in conflict between Islamic radicals and the army-backed authorities since the oil-producing North African state's promised transition from one-party rule to elected parliamentary government was sidetracked.
Zeroual, a former army general, is hoping to match the 75 percent turnout reported in the election which endorsed him in office in last year.
But analysts and diplomats said that hopes for change which flowered last year withered when violence continued and people felt the hardship of economic reforms required by overseas creditors.
"A year after the presidential election, political deadlock is still total," secular opposition leader Said Saadi said on Wednesday. "Social poverty is worsening every day."
This is Algeria's sixth referendum on constitutional reforms since independence from France in 1962.
Previous turnouts have been recorded as between 78 and 99 percent -- in the days when the National Liberation Front, leader of the independence struggle, held a monopoly on power.
This time opposition parties are telling supporters that if the draft is endorsed the result will be "institutional dictatorship".
The new constitution would bar politicians from campaigning on the basis of the Moslem faith, the Arab or Berber languages, gender issues or regional differences.
In northeastern, Berber-dominated areas a general strike against the proposed constitution started on Wednesday.
The draft makes Arabic sole official language of the state -- angering those who want Berber as an alternative.
Government ministers and their political backers crossed the country urging 16.4 million eligible voters to back the draft.

"Even before the results of the referendum are known. The conclusions on the future of democracy are far from being optimistic," said Algerian Liberte newspaper in a comment blasting the government for its tightened control on media from which opposition was barred.
